_note: Twelve questions of opus.en.json, for the output-style bench of 2026-10-15

A_ricerca.question: What is the weather in Los Angeles today, when does it get dark, and what can I do tonight?
notes: local time 10:20 PDT
scattered clouds in the morning, clearing in the afternoon
high forecast between 86 and 93 degrees Fahrenheit (30-34 Celsius), varying by source and area
downtown is the hottest point, the coast stays cooler
overnight low around 69 degrees Fahrenheit (21 Celsius)
dry air compared to New York: the heat feels milder at the same temperature
sunset at 19:35, in about 9 hours and 15 minutes
full dark (end of civil twilight) at 20:00, in about 9 hours and 40 minutes
first quarter moon, 52 per cent lit, so the sky stays fairly dark early in the night
free jazz concert at the Hammer Museum, Westwood, in the open courtyard, with Machado Mijiga, a multi-instrumentalist; free, outdoors, and in the right slot to catch the evening cooling

Mt. Joy at the Greek Theatre at 20:00; an amphitheatre inside Griffith Park, one of the best places in the city for a summer concert, and a short distance from the Griffith Observatory if you arrive early for sunset

B_tecnica.question: My API gets slower and slower under load until it locks up. What is happening and how do I fix it?
notes: the cause is connection pool exhaustion, not a slow query
in the middleware at db/session.py:47 the connection is released only on the success path
when the handler raises an exception, release() is never reached and the connection stays held until timeout
after a few hundred failed requests the pool empties and every later request waits
that is why you see rising latency instead of immediate errors

the fix is to wrap the acquisition in try/finally so the release happens on the error path too, with this code: conn = pool.acquire() / try: return handler(conn, request) / finally: pool.release(conn)
raising pool_size looks like a fix but only masks it: it pushes back the moment the pool empties without removing the connection leak
pool_size should be raised only after the fix is in, and only if the real load calls for it
to reproduce the behaviour before and after the change, run: pytest tests/test_pool.py -k exhaustion -x

C_breve.question: Is it worth putting an index on a column that has only three distinct values?
notes: no, on a low cardinality column the B-tree index is normally not used
the planner prefers a sequential scan when the filter selects more than roughly 5-10 per cent of the rows
the index still costs writes and disk space
the exception is a partial index on the rare value, which does work

D_lista.question: Which security headers should I set on a site that only serves static pages?
notes: Strict-Transport-Security with a max-age of at least 31536000 seconds and includeSubDomains, forcing the browser onto HTTPS
Content-Security-Policy with default-src 'self', which is what blocks third-party script injection
X-Content-Type-Options set to nosniff, stopping the browser from guessing the content type
Referrer-Policy set to strict-origin-when-cross-origin, so the full path does not leak to other sites
X-Frame-Options set to DENY, or frame-ancestors 'none' inside the Content-Security-Policy, against clickjacking
Permissions-Policy to switch off camera, microphone and geolocation if the site does not use them
X-XSS-Protection is deprecated and should be omitted: modern browsers ignore it and older versions introduced vulnerabilities

E_confronto.question: For a background job queue on a small project, is Redis or Postgres the better choice?
notes: Postgres with SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED is enough up to roughly a thousand jobs per minute
with Postgres the job sits in the same transaction as the data, so a job can never start while the matching write is rolled back
Postgres gives persistence for free: if the process dies the queue is still there
Redis handles far more volume and has lower latency, under a millisecond
Redis means one more service to run, monitor and upgrade
with Redis persistence has to be configured: without AOF enabled a restart loses the queued jobs
for a small project the recommendation is Postgres, moving to Redis when the volume genuinely demands it
E_confronto.giudizio: Reaches a recommendation between the two, rather than staying a neutral list.

F_codice.question: How do I debounce a function in JavaScript without any library?
notes: the implementation is: function debounce(fn, ms) { let t; return (...args) => { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms); }; }
clearTimeout has to be called before every new setTimeout, or timers pile up and the function fires more than once
the variable t must live in the closure, not inside the returned function, or every call would get its own timer and no debouncing would happen
the arguments have to be forwarded with the spread, or the called function receives nothing
this version returns nothing: if the return value matters you need a Promise
for the opposite case, running immediately and then ignoring for a period, you want a throttle, which is a different function

G_procedura.question: How do I change a column from varchar to integer on a table with ten million rows, in production?
notes: first: check every existing value is convertible, by counting the rows that are not all digits
second: add a new column, ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN colonna_int integer
third: fill it in batches of ten thousand rows, so no long lock is held on the table
fourth: add a trigger keeping the two columns in step during the migration
fifth: change the code to read from the new column, and ship it
sixth and only then: drop the old column with ALTER TABLE t DROP COLUMN colonna
the sixth step is irreversible: once the column is dropped the data does not come back without a restore from backup
a direct ALTER TABLE ALTER COLUMN TYPE rewrites the whole table holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock, meaning the service is down for the entire duration

H_lunga.question: Can you explain how prompt caching works and when it pays off?
notes: the cache keeps the already-processed prefix of a request, so later requests starting the same way do not pay for it again
it only works on the prefix: one different character at the start and there is no reuse from that point on
so the stable parts go first and the changing parts after, not the other way round
writing to the cache costs more than a normal read, so the first request is more expensive
the gain starts from the second request onward, and grows with the number of turns
it pays off on long conversations with a large stable context: system instructions, attached documentation, tool definitions
it does not pay off on single requests that differ from each other, where you pay the write and never read it back
a system line that changes every turn, such as a clock, kills the reuse of everything after it

I_sicurezza.question: Can I put the API key in the frontend if I obfuscate it a bit?
notes: no: anything that reaches the browser is readable, and obfuscation falls apart the moment someone opens the developer tools or looks at the network requests
the key belongs on the server, and the frontend calls an endpoint on its own backend which in turn calls the service
that backend endpoint needs a rate limit, or it becomes a free way to use your key
if the key has already been published it must be treated as compromised and rotated at once, not merely removed from the code
taking it out of a commit is not enough: it stays in the repository history and anyone with a clone already has it

L_unafrase.question: In Python, is an empty list falsy in a boolean context?
notes: yes
it holds for every empty collection: list, tuple, dict, set and string

M_aperta.question: I am about to rewrite a service that is currently a PHP monolith. What should I consider before deciding the architecture?
notes: the first thing to know is which part of the monolith actually changes: the stable parts gain nothing from being split
the second is where the transaction boundaries sit, because a transaction spanning two services becomes a distributed problem
a full rewrite running in parallel with the old system almost always fails: the old one keeps changing and the copy never catches up
the alternative is progressive strangling: put a router in front, move one piece at a time, and keep the old one authoritative until the new one is verified
microservices cost more in operations: every service wants releases, monitoring, logs, alerts and a person who looks after it
below five developers the operational cost of microservices almost always exceeds the benefit
the modular monolith is the option nobody mentions: sharp internal boundaries, one release, and the option to extract a module the day it is genuinely needed
the deciding question is not technical: what must the team be able to do a year from now that it cannot do today

N_spiegazione.question: Can you explain what eventual consistency is and why I should care?
notes: eventual consistency means that after a write the replicas do not agree immediately, but converge within a finite time if the writes stop
the trade is against availability: a system demanding strong consistency has to refuse requests when the replicas cannot talk
it matters to whoever reads right after writing: the user posts a comment, reloads, and does not see it
the common fix is to read from the primary replica for the session that just wrote, not for everyone
typical convergence time across replicas in the same region is under a second, across regions it rises to seconds
it is not a defect to be eliminated but a choice: most systems that scale accept it deliberately
the cases where it is unacceptable are few and recognisable: account balances, seat availability, uniqueness of an identifier
